report.tagline: A shopping and payments app that lets you split purchases into interest-free instalments, paid for mostly by the shops.
report.simpleSummary: Klarna lets you buy something now and pay for it later. At checkout on a site like ASOS or Sephora you pick Klarna and split a £90 purchase into three payments of £30, with no interest if you pay on time. The shop pays Klarna a fee because people buy more when they can split the cost. Klarna is now also a shopping app, a debit and credit card, and a savings account.

overview.whatItDoes: Klarna gives shoppers short, interest-free ways to pay in instalments and longer loans with interest for bigger buys. Shops pay Klarna a fee on each sale. It also runs a shopping app with deals and price tracking, a Klarna Card, and a savings and balance account, as it tries to become a full digital bank.
howItWorks: At checkout, the shopper chooses Klarna and picks Pay in 3 or 4, Pay in 30 days, or Financing over months.
Klarna runs a quick check in seconds and decides whether to approve this one purchase.
The shop gets paid in full right away, minus Klarna's fee. Klarna takes the risk that the shopper will not pay.
The shopper pays Klarna back through the app, usually by automatic card payments.
Klarna funds the loans mostly with deposits from its savings customers, which costs less than borrowing from banks.
Its AI assistant handles a large share of customer chats, which keeps support costs low.
overview.valueProposition: Shoppers spread the cost of a purchase without interest or a credit card. Shops sell more and get more customers through Klarna's app.

businessModel.summary: Klarna makes most of its money from shops, not shoppers. Shops pay a fee on each Klarna sale. Klarna also earns interest on longer loans, late fees, card fees, subscriptions and advertising. Its biggest costs are bad loans and the cost of funding the loans.

revenueStreams.detail: Shops pay a percentage plus a small fixed fee on every sale, often around 3% to 6%, more than a card payment costs them.
Longer Fair Financing loans charge interest to shoppers.
A small fee from the shop's bank each time the Klarna Card is used.
Merchants pay to promote products and deals in the Klarna app.
Paid plans and late fees in some markets. Subscription revenue grew more than 500% to $43 million in Q3 2026.

businessModel.pricing: Pay in 3 and Pay in 30 days are free for shoppers who pay on time. In the UK a missed payment can mean a late fee of up to £5. Financing interest varies by loan and country. Merchant fees are not fully public and are agreed with each shop.
costDrivers: Credit losses: shoppers who do not repay (provisions were 0.56% of volume in Q3 2026)
Funding costs: interest paid to savers and lenders to fund loans
Processing costs: card network and bank fees on each repayment
Staff and technology, reduced with AI
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take a £100 order paid in three parts. The shop pays Klarna about £4 to £5. Klarna pays maybe £1 for funding the money for six weeks and around £1 in processing costs. It expects to lose about 50p to 60p on average to people who do not pay. That leaves roughly £1.50 to £2.50 per order before staff and marketing. Klarna's 'transaction margin', revenue minus these direct costs, was $371 million on $36 billion of volume in Q3 2026, around 1% of volume. Profit comes from huge volume and keeping bad loans low.

howTheyGetUsers: Being shown at checkout on 1.35 million merchant sites
Partnerships with payment providers like Stripe, Adyen and Apple Pay, which put Klarna in front of more shops
The Klarna shopping app and deals
Big brand partners, for example Apple's device programmes and large US retailers
Marketing and celebrity campaigns in the US
whatBringsUsersBack: Saved details make the next Klarna checkout one tap
The Klarna Card for daily spending

growth.moat: Klarna has huge data on how millions of shoppers repay, which helps it approve the right people and keep losses low. Being on 1.35 million merchant checkouts and in a 122 million user app creates a network effect: more shoppers attract more shops, and more shops attract more shoppers. Its bank licence lets it fund loans cheaply with deposits.

competitors.name: Affirm
competitors.positioning: US leader in longer, interest-bearing loans and partner with Amazon and Shopify.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Klarna is larger globally and stronger in short interest-free plans; Affirm is bigger in US financing.

competitors.name: PayPal Pay in 3 / Pay in 4
competitors.positioning: BNPL built into PayPal checkout, free for merchants already on PayPal.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: PayPal has huge reach but BNPL is a side feature; Klarna is a full shopping app and card.

competitors.name: Clearpay (Afterpay)
competitors.positioning: Owned by Block; popular with fashion shoppers, linked to Cash App.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Klarna offers more payment types, including financing and a card.

competitors.name: Zilch
competitors.positioning: UK BNPL funded more by ads and merchant commissions.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Klarna has far more merchants and users; Zilch focuses on a card usable anywhere.

competitors.name: Credit cards
competitors.positioning: The traditional way to pay later, with interest after a grace period.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Klarna's short plans have no interest and approve people with no credit history.

northStar.metric: Number of purchases repaid on time by active users each month
northStar.why: It captures value for shoppers (they got what they wanted and could afford it), merchants (a completed sale) and Klarna (revenue with low losses). Counting only volume would reward lending to people who cannot pay. That is what makes it a good north star metric: it moves only when customers get real value.

pmLessons: Find who benefits most and charge them. Klarna made shops pay because they gain from higher sales.
Lending products live or die on risk. Growth without good approval decisions just creates losses.
Moving from one moment (checkout) to daily use (card, app) is how a feature becomes a platform.
AI can cut support costs, but users still need a human path when things go wrong.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you increase Klarna Card usage among existing app users?
interviewQuestions.hint: Segment users by how they use Klarna. Find barriers like awareness and trust. Ideas: rewards, default card in wallet, bill payments. Metric: card transactions per user. Guardrail: losses.

interviewQuestions.question: The FCA is regulating BNPL. What product changes would you make?
interviewQuestions.hint: Name the rules: affordability checks, clear terms. Make checks fast to keep conversion. Add spending controls. Measure conversion and complaints.

interviewQuestions.question: A big merchant wants a lower fee. How do you respond?
interviewQuestions.hint: Show value with data: conversion lift, order size, new customers from the app. Offer ads or tiers. Know your floor based on costs.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you measure whether the AI assistant is good?
interviewQuestions.hint: Resolution rate, repeat contacts, satisfaction, time to resolve, escalation rate. Compare to human support. Watch for silent failures.

interviewQuestions.question: Pick a north star for Klarna.
interviewQuestions.hint: Pick something that shows value to shoppers and merchants, like purchases repaid on time. Explain why GMV alone is risky in lending.
